messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Military Medic
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was forty-five, a military medic with twenty-two years of service, when the earthquake struck the coastal town where he'd been deployed on a humanitarian mission. The tremor lasted ninety seconds—a duration that had since become elastic in his mind, sometimes feeling like minutes. He had been in the clinic tent when the ground began to roll. The metal frame groaned and twisted; medical supplies cascaded from shelves. Around him, people screamed. A woman in labour seized his arm as the cot beneath her lurched sideways. Marcus had moved on instinct, bracing her, trying to steady the equipment, speaking in the calm voice that had carried him through two combat tours. But the ground would not obey him. It kept moving. The tent collapsed inward. Dust filled his lungs. For a moment—he was never quite sure how long—he could not see anything at all. When the shaking stopped, he was pinned beneath a metal pole, his left shoulder screaming, and the woman he had been trying to help was no longer moving. He had pulled himself free and crawled toward her, but by then the aftershocks had begun, and the world had fractured into a thousand disconnected moments that his mind could not arrange in any sensible order.

That was eight months ago. Now, in his small apartment in Portland, Marcus lived in a state of constant vigilance that exhausted him in ways that combat never had. Unexpected sounds—the neighbour's door slamming, a car backfiring, the sudden blare of a siren—sent his nervous system into overdrive. His heart would accelerate; his hands would tremble. He had come to believe that these sounds were warnings, that they carried the same unpredictability and threat as the rumbling that had preceded the collapse. He could not relax even when he sat alone in his living room with the doors locked and the lights on. His body refused to accept that he was safe. Some part of him remained in that tent, waiting for the ground to betray him again.

When memories of the event surfaced—and they came unbidden, without warning—Marcus was flooded with the same terror he had felt beneath the collapsed structure. The disorientation was total. He could recall the woman's face, the taste of dust, the weight of the pole, the sound of screaming, but they arrived in fragments that his mind could not assemble into a coherent narrative. The sequence had been scrambled. He would be reliving the moment of the collapse, then suddenly he was trying to find his way out of the tent, then he was on the ground beside the woman, then he was back at the beginning. The memories came without order or logic, and when they did, the emotion was so overwhelming that he would have to stop whatever he was doing—leave a conversation mid-sentence, pull his truck to the side of the road, excuse himself from the break room at the Veterans Affairs clinic where he still worked part-time. The terror on recall was indistinguishable from the original terror. His body did not know the difference between then and now.

What frightened Marcus most was that the meaning he had built his entire adult life around had dissolved. He had become a medic to save people. That had been his identity for more than two decades—the man who stayed steady, who knew what to do when everything fell apart. But he had not been able to save the woman in the tent. He had not even been able to keep himself from being trapped. Now, nothing felt meaningful anymore. The work he had done, the people he had helped, the sacrifices he had made—all of it seemed hollow, rendered pointless by a few seconds of geological violence that had reminded him that he was powerless. His entire framework for understanding the world—that skill and training and vigilance could protect you, that a life devoted to service had value—had been destroyed. And because he could no longer find meaning in anything, when the memories came, they carried even more weight. The terror was not just the physical sensation of being trapped; it was the existential weight of a life that no longer made sense. His shattered beliefs about how the world worked meant that the memories felt like proof of something darker: that chaos was the fundamental nature of reality, and that his attempts to impose order through service had been naive. This conviction deepened the terror each time the memory returned, and the overwhelming emotion that followed only reinforced his sense that the world was fundamentally unsafe and unknowable. Meanwhile, the constant threat he perceived in unexpected sounds kept him locked in a state of hypervigilance that made it harder to think, harder to work, harder to be around other people. He had begun to avoid the VA clinic when he could, making excuses to his supervisor. He had not seen his sister in three months, had not answered calls from old friends. The isolation was becoming its own kind of trap.

Marcus came to his first appointment with a therapist because his supervisor had made it a condition of keeping his job. He sat rigidly in the chair, his jaw clenched, listening to the sounds of the building around him—the hum of the fluorescent lights, the distant murmur of voices in the hallway—as if they might at any moment betray him. He was not sure therapy could help. He was not sure anything could. What he wanted, though he did not quite say it, was to feel like himself again. To know who that person was.
